claims.text: The proposed starting alloy is an equiatomic Ti20Zr20Hf20Mo20Cr20 high-entropy alloy.
Rapid quenching of Ti20Zr20Hf20Mo20Cr20 yields a maximally random, fully disordered solid solution with minimal short-range order.
Annealing at 600°C for 48 hours will enhance short-range chemical order in the proposed alloy.
Annealing and suitable chemical interactions can drive local chemical ordering in nearly random multicomponent alloys.
The annealed and quenched samples can remain single-phase BCC or FCC materials after the proposed treatment.
Short-range order in this alloy will consist of preferential local clustering or ordering of Hf and Mo relative to Ti, Zr, and Cr.
Short-range chemical order will alter the local electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
The ordering-induced change in the density of states will enhance electron-phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling will strengthen Cooper pairing and increase the superconducting transition temperature.
The annealed alloy will have a higher superconducting transition temperature than the rapidly quenched baseline.
Annealing-induced short-range order may alter the upper and lower critical magnetic fields.
Changes in transition temperature or critical fields would indicate that short-range order modified electron-phonon coupling.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase high-entropy alloys containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, provided phase segregation is absent.
High-resolution electron microscopy and atom probe tomography can be used to characterize local chemical ordering.
Comparing resistivity, magnetic susceptibility, and critical fields between annealed and rapidly quenched samples provides a controlled superconductivity test.
Failure of a single-phase annealed sample to show an increase in transition temperature would falsify the directional hypothesis.
Degradation of superconducting properties after annealing would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis predicts an increase in Tc, but the predicted outcome is broadened to an increase or any distinct variation. The falsification rule then treats degradation as falsifying, even though degradation could qualify as a distinct variation under the broader prediction.
